content_of_post_to_comment:
tbh my brain felt completely fried for the first half of this year. couldn't read 5 pages of a book, couldn't focus on work for 15 minutes without pulling up shorts or switching tabs. i was even watching youtube videos on 1.5x or 2x speed thinking i was "optimizing my time" when really i was just addicted to constant stimulation.

tried all the standard advice people throw around—pomodoro timers, app blockers, cold showers. none of it stuck because i was still fighting my own dopamine tolerance.

a few weeks ago i stumbled on a random video essay late at night about how modern content destroys attention spans. I usually scroll past those motivational rants, but the editing and pacing on this one were different. it laid out a few things that actually clicked for me:

wishes vs decisions: i kept making vague "wishes" (i need to lock in today and be productive) instead of concrete "decisions" (phone goes in the other room for 20 mins). if an action requires feeling motivated first, it’s just a wish.

the 2x speed trap: watching self-help at double speed gives you a fake sense of accomplishment. you’re not actually absorbing anything, you're just chasing fast info without any quiet processing time.

making the start stupidly small: if your focus is dead, aiming for a 2-hour deep work block guarantees failure. you have to lower the entry barrier until refusing to do it feels dumber than just starting.

been trying this out for about 2-3 weeks now and it’s honestly the first time in forever i can sit down and get actual work done without itching for my phone every 2 minutes.
comment: The phone-in-another-room decision is such a practical shift. I’ve noticed the same thing with focus: relying on willpower keeps turning every task into a negotiation. Removing the choice entirely helps because you’re not constantly spending energy deciding whether to check something. The small-start idea also seems underrated because momentum usually shows up after you begin, not before.
